tagline: The story of David's reign over Israel: how the shepherd became king, how God promised him a house that would last forever, and how his own sin tore that house apart.
overview:
Second Samuel picks up the story the day after Saul dies on Mount Gilboa and follows David for the rest of his life as king. It opens with a lament rather than a victory song. David is first crowned by his own tribe of Judah at Hebron, while Saul's surviving son rules the northern tribes, and a slow civil war grinds on until the northern leaders are killed and all Israel comes to Hebron to make David king. He captures Jerusalem, makes it his capital, brings the ark of the covenant there, defeats the Philistines and the surrounding peoples, and receives from God, through the prophet Nathan, a promise that his dynasty and throne will endure forever.

Then, at the height of his power, David takes Bathsheba, the wife of one of his own soldiers, and arranges her husband's death. Nathan confronts him, David confesses, and God forgives him, but the consequences run through the rest of the book. His son Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar; her brother Absalom kills Amnon, goes into exile, returns, and eventually drives David out of Jerusalem in a rebellion that ends with Absalom's death and David's bitter grief. A further revolt follows. The book closes with a collection of stories, lists, and poems, including David's great song of deliverance and his last words, and ends with David buying the threshing floor where the temple will one day stand.

Second Samuel matters because it gives the Bible both its highest picture of a king and its most honest. The covenant with David in chapter 7 becomes the root of Israel's hope for a coming king, the Messiah. The same book refuses to hide what that king did with his power. Read together with 1 Samuel (they are one book in the Hebrew Bible), it asks what faithful rule looks like and shows that even the best human king cannot finally be the answer.
author:
The book is anonymous, and since Samuel died in 1 Samuel 25, he can't be its author. A Jewish tradition recorded in the Babylonian Talmud credits the books of Samuel to Samuel himself with completion by the prophets Gad and Nathan, which draws on 1 Chronicles 29:29 and its mention of records kept by Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the seer. Both Nathan and Gad appear in 2 Samuel, and many readers take the Chronicles verse as a sign that written prophetic sources lay behind the book.

Modern scholars generally see 2 Samuel as built from earlier sources. Leonhard Rost, in 1926, argued that chapters 9 to 20, together with 1 Kings 1 and 2, form a single Succession Narrative (sometimes called the Court History of David) that explains how Solomon came to the throne. Many also see the end of a History of David's Rise in the first chapters of the book, and treat chapters 21 to 24 as a separate appendix. Since Martin Noth's work in 1943, many have read Samuel as part of a larger Deuteronomistic History (Deuteronomy through Kings) brought to its final form around the time of the Babylonian exile. More conservative scholars stress the vivid, eyewitness quality of the court narrative and place its main composition close to the events. Whatever the sources, the finished book is a deliberate and skillfully shaped work.
date:
The events cover David's reign, which the book gives as forty years: seven years and six months at Hebron over Judah and thirty-three years at Jerusalem over all Israel (2 Samuel 5:4-5). His reign is usually placed around 1010 to 970 BC, with the capture of Jerusalem a few years into it; these dates are approximate.

The writing is later than the events, though how much later is debated. Scholars who read Samuel within the Deuteronomistic History date its final edition to the late seventh or the sixth century BC, while granting that sources such as the court narrative are much older, possibly from the time of Solomon. Others place most of the book within a century or so of David. The Dead Sea Scrolls include manuscripts of Samuel, the best preserved being 4QSamuel-a, whose wording often agrees with the Greek Septuagint against the standard Hebrew text, a reminder that the book circulated in more than one textual form before the time of Christ.
setting:
David's reign falls in a window when no great empire controlled the land between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Egypt was weak and divided, and Assyria had not yet begun the westward expansion that would dominate the ninth and eighth centuries BC. That vacuum left room for small kingdoms: the Philistine city-states on the coast, the Aramean states to the north around Damascus and Zobah, and Ammon, Moab, and Edom east and south of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. Second Samuel shows David defeating or subduing most of these and making alliances with others, such as Hiram, king of the Phoenician port city of Tyre.

Inside Israel, the old tribal loyalties remained strong. Judah in the south and the tribes of the north (often simply called Israel) had separate identities, and the book repeatedly shows the seam between them: David rules Judah first, the north joins him by covenant, and later revolts draw on northern resentment. Jerusalem, a Jebusite city that no tribe had held, gave David a capital that belonged to neither side. Outside the Bible, the Tel Dan inscription, an Aramaic victory stele found in northern Israel in 1993 and 1994 and dated to the ninth century BC, refers to the king of the house of David, most scholars agree, which shows that a dynasty traced to David was known to Israel's neighbors within about a century and a half of his death.
purpose: Second Samuel explains how David's dynasty came to rule Israel and why God's promise rested on it. For its first readers, whether in the days of the kings or in exile after Jerusalem fell, it answered urgent questions: Is the house of David legitimate? What has become of God's promise to it? Why did things go so wrong? The book defends David against the charge that he seized Saul's throne by violence, carefully showing him innocent of the deaths of Saul, Abner, and Ish-bosheth. It is equally careful to show his guilt where he was guilty. The purpose isn't propaganda but testimony: God's promise holds even when the king fails, and the king is not above God's word. For readers who had lost their king and land, the unconditional promise of 2 Samuel 7 was a reason to keep hoping.
story: First Samuel told how Israel moved from judges to kings, how Saul was chosen and rejected, and how David was anointed and waited in the wilderness for a throne he refused to take by force. Second Samuel shows that throne given, the kingdom united and secured, Jerusalem made the city of God, and the covenant made with David's house. It also shows the start of the troubles that will split the kingdom after Solomon. First Kings continues directly, with David's old age, Solomon's accession, and the building of the temple on the site David bought at the end of this book. The promise of chapter 7 then echoes through the Psalms, the prophets, and the New Testament.
christ: The New Testament's first line calls Jesus the son of David (Matthew 1:1), and that title reaches back to this book. In 2 Samuel 7 God promises David, “I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom”, and adds, “I will be his Father, and he will be My son.” The promise first applies to Solomon, who will build the temple, but its word forever stretched Israel's hope beyond any one king, especially after the line of kings ended in exile. The prophets looked for a coming son of David (Isaiah 9 and 11, Jeremiah 23, Ezekiel 34), and the New Testament proclaims Jesus as that king: Gabriel tells Mary that God will give her son the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32-33), Paul describes Jesus as descended from David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), and Hebrews 1:5 applies the Father and son words of 2 Samuel 7:14 to Christ. The book also shows what the coming king must be that David was not. David is a shepherd king, but he abuses his power, sheds innocent blood, and cannot govern his own house. The longing the book leaves is for a son of David who is righteous as David was not.
reading:
Read 2 Samuel as narrative history told with great artistic restraint. The narrator rarely comments and seldom says what characters feel or what God thinks of an action; he lets speeches, silences, and repeated words carry the meaning. When he does speak directly, as in 11:27, where he says that what David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD, it lands with full weight. Watch for echoes: David's sin with Bathsheba sets off a chain of sexual violence, murder, and rebellion within his own family that answers his crime, just as Nathan said it would.

Two misreadings are common. One is to make David a simple moral hero whose every act is a model; the book itself does not allow that. The other is to read him cynically as a ruthless politician whose piety is only a mask; the book shows real faith, real repentance, and real grief. Also notice that chapters 21 to 24 are not in chronological order but form a carefully arranged appendix, with two narratives on the outside, two lists of warriors inside those, and two poems at the center.

structure.title: David king over Judah
structure.summary: David mourns Saul and Jonathan and is anointed king of Judah at Hebron. A long civil war with the house of Saul ends when Abner and Ish-bosheth are murdered, killings David publicly disowns.

structure.title: The kingdom established
structure.summary: All Israel makes David king. He takes Jerusalem, brings up the ark, receives God's covenant promise of an everlasting house, defeats his enemies, and shows kindness to Jonathan's son Mephibosheth.

structure.title: David's sin and Nathan's rebuke
structure.summary: David commits adultery with Bathsheba and has Uriah killed. Nathan confronts him with a parable, David confesses, and God forgives him but announces that the sword will not depart from his house.

structure.title: Troubles in David's house
structure.summary: Amnon rapes Tamar, Absalom murders Amnon, and after years of estrangement Absalom leads a rebellion that drives David from Jerusalem. Absalom dies, David returns, and a further revolt under Sheba is put down.

structure.title: Appendix: David's reign in retrospect
structure.summary: A deliberately arranged collection: a famine and the Gibeonites, lists of David's warriors, his song of deliverance and last words, and the census and plague that end at the threshing floor of Araunah.

themes.title: God's covenant with David
themes.body: The center of the book is chapter 7, where God refuses David's offer to build him a house and promises instead to build David a house: a dynasty, a kingdom, and a throne established forever. God will discipline David's sons when they do wrong but will never withdraw his loving devotion as he did from Saul. This promise shapes the rest of the Old Testament and becomes the ground of the hope for the Messiah.

themes.title: Power received, not seized
themes.body: The first chapters of the book go to great lengths to show that David did not take the throne by murder. Each person who hopes to win his favor by killing a rival (the Amalekite, Joab, Rechab and Baanah) is rebuked or executed. David waits for God and for the people. The book presents this as the mark of a true king, and it makes the later chapters, where David himself grasps what is not his, all the more shocking.

themes.title: Sin, confession, and consequences
themes.body: David's adultery and murder are told without excuse. When Nathan confronts him, David confesses plainly, and God forgives him at once. Forgiveness, however, does not undo what his sin set loose. The book traces those consequences through his family with painful honesty, holding together real grace and real cost in a way that resists both cheap forgiveness and despair.

themes.title: The LORD in the midst of his people
themes.body: David brings the ark to Jerusalem and wants to build a temple for it. The ark's arrival is joyful but dangerous, as Uzzah's death shows: the holy God cannot be handled carelessly. The book ends with David choosing mercy from God's hand rather than from human hands, and buying the site where sacrifice stops the plague, pointing ahead to the temple.

themes.title: The king under God's word
themes.body: In the ancient world kings often stood above any law. In 2 Samuel the prophet Nathan can walk into the palace and say to the king, “You are that man!” The king is accountable to the LORD and to his covenant. This conviction, that power stands under God's judgment, runs through the whole story of Israel's kings.

keyChapters.why: David's lament over Saul and Jonathan sets the tone for his reign: he grieves the king who hunted him rather than celebrating his fall.
All Israel anoints David king, and he captures Jerusalem, which becomes the City of David and the center of Israel's life and hope.
The ark comes to Jerusalem amid joy and danger, joining the throne of David to the presence of the LORD.
God's covenant with David promises an everlasting house, kingdom, and throne, the root of the Bible's hope for the Messiah.
David's adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah mark the turning point of his reign and of the book.
Nathan's parable confronts the king, David confesses, and God forgives him while announcing the consequences that will follow.
Absalom's death and David's grief over him show the full cost of the sword that would not depart from his house.
David's song of deliverance, nearly identical to Psalm 18, gathers the whole story into praise of God as rock and refuge.

parts.body:
Second Samuel is the tenth book of the Bible. It has 24 chapters, and it tells the story of David's reign, from the day after Saul's death on Mount Gilboa to David's last years.

It moves in three arcs. First the throne comes to David without his grasping for it. Judah makes him king at Hebron, the house of Saul fades in a slow civil war, all Israel comes to him, and he takes Jerusalem and brings the ark of God there. Then, at the height of his power, David takes another man's wife and has her husband killed. After that the book follows what his sin set loose in his own family: a daughter raped by her half-brother, a son murdered at his brother's order, a revolt that drives the king from his city, and a father weeping for the son who tried to take his throne. The last four chapters gather songs, lists and stories from across the reign.

Some of the Bible's best-known scenes are here: David's lament, ‘How the mighty have fallen’ (1:19), the king dancing before the ark, a prophet's story about a poor man's lamb and his words to the king, “You are that man!” (12:7), and the cry “O my son Absalom!” (18:33).

At the center stands a promise. David wants to build a house for God, and God answers that he will build David a house, a line of kings: “Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever” (7:16). The rest of the Bible keeps coming back to that sentence.

Second Samuel gives the Bible both its highest picture of a king and its most honest. It shows a king whom God chose and loved, and it refuses to hide what that king did with his power.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Second Samuel picks up the day after 1 Samuel ends. Saul and Jonathan lie dead on Mount Gilboa, the Philistines hold much of the north, and David, who would not lift his hand against Saul, is waiting at Ziklag.

In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Samuel are one book. The Greek translation made by Jews before the time of Jesus, the Septuagint, divided it in two and counted it with Kings as the four books of the Kingdoms, and printed Hebrew Bibles later followed. With Joshua, Judges and Kings, Samuel belongs to what the Hebrew Bible calls the Former Prophets, which tell Israel's story in the land and measure each generation by the covenant.

Second Samuel is the high point of that story and the place where it turns. The kingdom is united, Jerusalem becomes the city of God, and God binds himself to David's house. But the troubles in David's family run on into 1 Kings, which follows without a break with David's old age and Solomon's rise. Solomon's temple will stand on the threshing floor David buys in the last chapter.

The same years are told again in 1 Chronicles 11 to 29, written after the exile. Chronicles leaves out David's adultery, the murder of Uriah and the revolt of Absalom. Samuel tells the story with its wounds open.

And the promise of chapter 7 keeps sounding. Psalm 89 sings it back to God, the prophets look for a righteous branch for David (Jeremiah 23:5), and the New Testament's first line calls Jesus the son of David (Matthew 1:1).

The book does not name its author, and Samuel, who dies in 1 Samuel 25, cannot have written it. A Jewish tradition preserved in the Babylonian Talmud credits the books of Samuel to Samuel, completed by the prophets Gad and Nathan. It draws on 1 Chronicles 29:29, which names records kept by Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and many readers take that verse as a sign that prophets' records lay behind the book.

Modern scholars generally see the book as built from earlier accounts. In 1926 Leonhard Rost argued that chapters 9 to 20, with 1 Kings 1 and 2, form one story, often called the Succession Narrative, which explains how Solomon came to the throne. Many also find the end of a history of David's rise in the first chapters, and treat chapters 21 to 24 as a separate collection. Since the German scholar Martin Noth's work in 1943, many have read Samuel as part of one larger history from Deuteronomy to Kings, given its final form around the time of the exile in Babylon. Others place most of the book within a century or so of David. More conservative scholars stress the vivid, close detail of the court story and place its writing near the events.

The text has a history too. The best-preserved copy of Samuel among the Dead Sea Scrolls, called 4QSamuel-a, often agrees with the Greek translation against the standard Hebrew, a sign that the book circulated in more than one form before the time of Christ. The standard Hebrew of 15:7 says forty years, which cannot fit David's reign; some Greek copies and the Syriac read four, and the Berean Standard Bible follows them. The Greek, and a fragment of Samuel among the scrolls, add a line to 13:21 saying why David did not punish Amnon.

Christians who receive 2 Samuel as God's word hold more than one of these views, and these notes take no side among them. On every view, the finished book is carefully and skillfully shaped.

parts.h: David's world, and what has been dug up
parts.body:
David's reign is usually dated to about 1010 to 970 BC. The book gives him forty years: seven and a half at Hebron over Judah, and thirty-three at Jerusalem over all Israel and Judah (5:4-5). Counting back from the division of the kingdom around 931 BC gives those dates, though the round forty may be approximate, as forty often is in the Bible.

His reign fell in a window when no great empire held the land between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Egypt was weak and divided, and Assyria had not yet begun its push west. That left room for small kingdoms: the Philistine cities on the coast, the Aramean states of Damascus and Zobah to the north, and Ammon, Moab and Edom across the Jordan and the Dead Sea. Second Samuel shows David subduing most of them and making an ally of Hiram, king of Tyre (5:11).

Inside Israel the old tribal loyalties ran deep. Judah in the south and the northern tribes kept separate identities, and the book keeps showing the seam: David rules Judah first, the north joins him by covenant, and later revolts draw on northern resentment. Jerusalem was a Jebusite city that no tribe had held (Joshua 15:63), so it gave David a capital that belonged to neither side.

A massive stepped stone structure has been uncovered on the slope of the City of David, but its date and its relation to David are debated. A shaft Charles Warren found in 1867 was long linked with the ‘water shaft’ of 5:8, but later excavations suggest it was not accessible in David's time.

Outside the Bible, David's line is named. An Aramaic victory inscription found at Tel Dan in 1993 and 1994, most likely set up by Hazael of Damascus in the second half of the ninth century BC, refers to a king of the house of David. Most scholars take it as the earliest known reference to David's dynasty by name. How large his kingdom was is argued. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, in David and Solomon (2006), argued that tenth-century Judah was a thinly settled highland chiefdom and that the Bible's picture was magnified later. Others point to Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town above the Elah Valley excavated from 2007 and dated to the early tenth century BC, as evidence of organized rule in Judah in David's time. The site's page on what archaeology shows gives the balance: on the size of David's kingdom the evidence is thin and argued over, and it neither proves the biblical account nor shows it false. These notes claim no more for what has been found than it shows.

The book falls into five parts: David king over Judah (chapters 1 to 4); the kingdom established, with Jerusalem, the ark and God's promise (5 to 10); David's sin and Nathan's rebuke (11 and 12); the troubles in David's house, from the rape of Tamar to the revolts of Absalom and Sheba (13 to 20); and a closing collection (21 to 24).

Chapters 11 and 12 are the hinge. Before them, nearly everything David touches prospers. After them, the sword Nathan foretold never leaves his house (12:10). The same king, the same God and the same promise stand on both sides.

The narrator tells the story with great restraint. He seldom says what people feel or what God thinks, and lets speeches, silences and repeated words carry the meaning. Watch the word house, which means a building, a household and a line of kings, and is the key to chapter 7; the verbs send and take in chapter 11; and the sword after it.

The last four chapters are not in the order of events. They are a carefully arranged collection: two stories on the outside, a famine in chapter 21 and a plague in chapter 24; two lists of David's warriors inside those; and two poems at the center, David's song of rescue and his last words.

The book takes care to show that David did not seize Saul's throne by violence, and that he was innocent of the deaths of Saul, Abner and Ish-bosheth. It is just as careful to show his guilt where he was guilty.

parts.h: King at Hebron: a crown not seized
parts.body:
The book opens with a man who thinks he brings good news. An Amalekite arrives with Saul's crown and armband and says that he killed the wounded king at Saul's own request (1:10). His story does not match the account of Saul's death in 1 Samuel 31, and most readers conclude that he found the body and made up the rest to win a reward. David mourns, and then has him put to death for claiming to have destroyed ‘the LORD’s anointed’ (1:14).

Then David sings his lament for Saul and Jonathan, the Song of the Bow, one of the Old Testament's great poems. He grieves the king who hunted him, and of Jonathan he says, “your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women” (1:26). Most readers, ancient and modern, hear the language of deep covenant friendship; some modern readers hear a romantic bond. The chapter note sets out both.

The men of Judah anoint David king at Hebron (2:4). Saul's commander Abner makes Saul's son Ish-bosheth king over the rest of Israel, and ‘the war between the house of Saul and the house of David was protracted’ (3:1). Later Abner, who had killed Joab's brother Asahel in battle, offers to bring all Israel over to David, and after a peaceful meeting at Hebron, Joab lures him back and kills him. David curses Joab and mourns Abner, and admits, “And I am weak this day, though anointed as king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too fierce for me” (3:39). Then two of Ish-bosheth's own captains murder him in his bed and bring his head to David, who has them put to death.

In these chapters each man who kills one of David's rivals, to win his favor or for his own ends, is rebuked or put to death. David waits for God and for the people. The book presents this as the mark of a true king, and it makes the later chapters, where David grasps what is not his, all the more shocking.

One small puzzle: Saul's son Ish-bosheth and Jonathan's son Mephibosheth are called Eshbaal and Merib-baal in 1 Chronicles. Most scholars think scribes replaced baal, which could simply mean lord, with bosheth, shame, because Baal was also the name of a Canaanite god.

After seven and a half years the northern tribes come to Hebron. “Here we are, your own flesh and blood” (5:1), they say, and they remind David of the LORD's word: ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them’ (5:2). The elders make a covenant with him before the LORD and anoint him king over all Israel.

His first act is to take Jerusalem. The Jebusites taunt him that even the blind and lame could hold him off, and David captures ‘the fortress of Zion’ and calls it the City of David (5:6-9). The saying about the blind and the lame in 5:8 is among the hardest verses in Samuel to translate, and the chapter note sets out how it has been read. Whatever it meant, the same book shows David seating Jonathan's son, lame in both feet, at his own table for life (9:13).

Then David brings the ark of God up to Jerusalem, joining his throne to the presence of the LORD. The first attempt ends in disaster. The ark rides on a new cart, the oxen stumble, Uzzah takes hold of the ark, and ‘God struck him down on the spot’ (6:7). David is angry and afraid, and the ark waits three months in the house of Obed-edom, where ‘the LORD blessed him and all his household’ (6:11). The second time the ark is carried, and David, in a linen ephod, ‘danced with all his might before the LORD’ (6:14). His wife Michal, Saul's daughter, watches from a window and despises him.

Uzzah's death has long troubled readers. Some stress that the procession ignored the law, which said the holy things were to be carried by Levites and not touched (Numbers 4:15), as David himself says in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 15:13). Some read it as a sign that God will not be used as a political symbol at the moment his ark enters the king's city. None of these removes the shock, and the chapter does not hide David's anger. It asks a reader to take God's holiness seriously.

In chapter 8 the LORD gives David victory on every side, and ‘David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people’ (8:15).

Chapter 7 is the center of the book. Settled in his palace, David says to the prophet Nathan, “Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God remains in a tent” (7:2). He wants to build God a temple, and Nathan agrees. That night God answers through Nathan. He took David from following the flock to be ruler over his people. And he turns David's offer around: ‘He Himself will establish a house for you’ (7:11).

In Hebrew, house can mean a building, a palace, a temple, a household or a line of kings, and the chapter uses every sense. Then come words that echo through the rest of the Bible: “I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his Father, and he will be My son” (7:12-14). When this son does wrong, God will discipline him, ‘But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul’ (7:15).

David goes in and sits before the LORD, and his prayer begins, “Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?” (7:18). The chapter never uses the word covenant, but David's last words call the promise ‘an everlasting covenant’ (23:5).

The son of 7:12-15 is first Solomon, who builds the temple (1 Kings 8:20). But forever reached beyond him. After Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, no descendant of David ruled again, and Psalm 89 holds the promise up to God: “You have renounced the covenant with Your servant and sullied his crown in the dust” (Psalm 89:39). Frank Moore Cross argued in 1973 that the history had two editions, one confident in the promise and a later one, in the exile, that added its conditions. Some readers hold that the promise always carried a condition for each king and a guarantee for the line. The prophets kept it alive, speaking of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1).

Before there were Christians, Jews were reading the promise of a son of David to come. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a text called 4QFlorilegium, copied in the late first century BC, quotes 7:10-14 of the Branch of David who will arise in the last days, and the Psalms of Solomon, written after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, pray for God to raise up the son of David as king. Jewish prayer still asks God to make the shoot of David flourish. Christians confess that the promise is kept in Jesus. Jewish and Christian readers part over how it is fulfilled, and that difference deserves to be stated with respect.

Chapter 11 opens in the spring of a war: ‘David sent out Joab and his servants with the whole army of Israel ... but David remained in Jerusalem’ (11:1). From his palace roof he sees a woman bathing, and he is told who she is: Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his own soldiers, away at the war. “Then David sent messengers to get her, and when she came to him, he slept with her” (11:4).

The verbs belong to David: he sees, he sends, he takes, he lies with her. Bathsheba speaks only once, to send him word: “I am pregnant” (11:5). Readers have asked whether she was a willing partner or a victim of the king's power. A woman summoned by the king's messengers had little power to refuse, and the text places the whole responsibility on David. Nothing in the story blames her.

David tries to cover what he has done. He brings Uriah home from the front, and Uriah will not go to his house while the army sleeps in the field. So David sends him back to Joab with a letter: “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed” (11:15). Uriah dies, and David marries his widow. Then the narrator gives his verdict: “But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD” (11:27).

The LORD sends the prophet Nathan, who tells the king about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb. David burns with anger at the rich man, and Nathan answers, “You are that man!” (12:7). In much of the ancient world kings stood above the law. Here a prophet with nothing but a word from God names the king's crime to his face.

David does not argue. “I have sinned against the LORD,” he says, and Nathan replies, “The LORD has taken away your sin” (12:13). Forgiveness comes at once. But the sword will never depart from David's house (12:10), and the LORD strikes the child born to Bathsheba, and the child dies. It is one of the hardest lines in Samuel, and the chapter note does not soften it. Afterward Bathsheba bears Solomon, and the LORD sends word to name him Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD (12:24-25).

Psalm 51 carries a heading that sets it ‘When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba’ (Psalm 51:1), and it has been prayed for many centuries by people who were sure they had gone too far. Much later the book of Kings calls David faithful ‘except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite’ (1 Kings 15:5).

Nathan's word begins to come true in the next chapter, with the worst. David's eldest son Amnon becomes obsessed with his half-sister Tamar. On a cousin's advice he pretends to be ill, and David himself sends Tamar to Amnon's house to cook for him (13:7). There Amnon rapes her. She pleads with him, “such a thing should never be done in Israel” (13:12), ‘But Amnon refused to listen to her, and being stronger, he violated her’ (13:14). Then he hates her and has her thrown out. Tamar tears her royal robe and goes away crying bitterly. Her brother Absalom tells her to be quiet, and she lives on ‘as a desolate woman in the house of her brother Absalom’ (13:20). “When King David heard all this, he was furious” (13:21), and he did nothing.

The Bible tells this story with all its sympathy on Tamar's side, and it gives her the chapter's clearest moral voice. The wrong was Amnon's alone, and the shame she feared belonged to him. The chapter also exposes the men around her: a cousin who planned it, a brother who silenced her, and a father who was angry and did not act.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Two years later Absalom has Amnon killed at a sheepshearing feast and flees to his grandfather, the king of Geshur. After three years Joab sends a wise woman of Tekoa to move the king, and Absalom comes home, but David will not see him for two more years.

Absalom then spends years winning the people: ‘In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel’ (15:6). He has himself proclaimed king at Hebron, and David flees Jerusalem on foot, weeping as he climbs the Mount of Olives (15:30). On the road Shimei of Saul's family curses him, and David will not let him be killed. In Jerusalem, on the advice of David's own counselor Ahithophel, Absalom sleeps with his father's concubines in a tent on the palace roof, in the sight of all Israel (16:22). Nathan had said that it would happen (12:11-12). The judgment fell on David, but ten women bore it, and the text never gives them a voice.

The LORD defeats Ahithophel's counsel (17:14), and David escapes across the Jordan. In the forest of Ephraim, Absalom's army is routed. David has ordered his commanders to deal gently with his son, but Joab kills Absalom as he hangs caught in a tree. When the news comes, the king goes up to the room over the gate and weeps: “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!” (18:33).

David returns, but the kingdom is split. Judah and Israel quarrel over the king, a Benjamite named Sheba calls the north away, and Joab murders his rival Amasa on the road. The ten women are shut away for the rest of their lives (20:3). The sword has not left David's house.

parts.h: Famine, songs, heroes and a threshing floor
parts.body:
The last four chapters step back from the story. They begin with a famine, which the LORD traces to the blood Saul shed when he tried to wipe out the Gibeonites, a people Israel had sworn by the LORD to spare in Joshua's day (21:1-2). The Gibeonites ask for seven of Saul's descendants, and David hands them over to be put to death. It is one of the hardest passages in the historical books. The text says that the LORD named the cause of the famine; it does not say that he commanded the deaths. The law forbade putting children to death for their fathers' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16), and the chapter note sets out how readers weigh the story. What the chapter plainly honors is a grieving mother. Rizpah, the mother of two of the men, spreads sackcloth on a rock and guards their bodies from the beginning of the harvest until the rain (21:10), and her faithfulness moves the king to give them, with the bones of Saul and Jonathan, an honorable burial.

Four brief battle reports follow, in which David's men kill Philistine giants. One says that Elhanan of Bethlehem killed ‘the brother of Goliath the Gittite’ (21:19), words supplied from 1 Chronicles 20:5; the standard Hebrew of Samuel names Goliath himself, and the site's page on Samuel and Chronicles sets out the explanations.

At the center stand two poems. Chapter 22 is David's song of rescue, almost the same as Psalm 18: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer” (22:2). It ends, ‘He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever’ (22:51). Chapter 23 gives David's last words, about the ruler who governs justly, ‘like the light of the morning at sunrise’ (23:4). Around the poems run the lists of David's mighty men. Three of them broke through Philistine lines to bring him water from the well at Bethlehem, and he poured it out to the LORD as the blood of men who had risked their lives (23:15-17). The list ends with a name: ‘and Uriah the Hittite’ (23:39).

The book closes with a census and a plague. ‘Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He stirred up David against them’ (24:1). The same story in 1 Chronicles 21:1 names Satan as the one who incited David, and many readers take the two together: God permitting or using an adversary's temptation as part of a judgment, while David freely chose and answered for what he did. David confesses and chooses to fall into the hands of the LORD, ‘for His mercies are great’ (24:14). Seventy thousand die before the LORD stops the angel at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, and David pleads, “Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done?” (24:17). He buys the floor rather than take it as a gift: “I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing” (24:24). The temple would one day stand on that ground.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads 2 Samuel
parts.body:
The New Testament names David often, and it is wise to keep to the lines it draws.

Most of all it reads chapter 7 of Jesus. The angel tells Mary that God will give her son ‘the throne of His father David’ and that ‘His kingdom will never end’ (Luke 1:32-33). Peter at Pentecost says that David knew God ‘had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne’ (Acts 2:30). Paul at Pisidian Antioch moves from David to Jesus: “From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised” (Acts 13:23), and he opens Romans by calling God's Son ‘a descendant of David according to the flesh’ (Romans 1:3). Hebrews quotes the promise itself of Christ: “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son” (Hebrews 1:5).

The New Testament does not deny that the promise first meant Solomon. Hebrews quotes only the first half of 7:14 and leaves out the words about discipline for wrongdoing, which fit Solomon and the kings after him and not Jesus. The promise is fulfilled across a history, not in a single prediction.

Other lines are drawn too. Matthew's family tree names Bathsheba only as ‘Uriah’s wife’ (Matthew 1:6), keeping Uriah's name, and David's sin, inside the line of the Messiah. Luke traces Jesus' line through Nathan, a son of David born in Jerusalem (Luke 3:31; 2 Samuel 5:14). Matthew ends his quotation of Micah with words God spoke to David, ‘who will be the shepherd of My people Israel’ (Matthew 2:6; 2 Samuel 5:2). Paul quotes a line from the end of David's song, in its twin, Psalm 18 (Romans 15:9), and Psalm 51, David's prayer after his sin with Bathsheba (Romans 3:4).

Second Samuel does not predict Jesus in detail, and these notes make no scene in David's life a picture of him beyond what the New Testament says. It gives the promise, and the words son of David and anointed, in which the church confessed him.

Second Samuel is Israel's Scripture first. Jewish readers still look for a son of David to come, and their reading deserves to be stated fairly. The book records Israel's king and his sins as honestly as Israel's own prophets did, and nothing in it, or in the New Testament's use of it, is a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people.

A few habits will help a new reader.

Read chapter 7 slowly; the rest of the Bible keeps coming back to it.

Watch for the narrator's verdicts. He tells most of the story without comment, so when he speaks, as at the end of chapter 11, it lands with full weight.

Do not take David as a model in everything, and do not read him as a schemer whose faith was a mask. The book shows real faith, real repentance and real grief, and a king who abused his power, shed innocent blood and could not govern his own house.

Read the psalms the book brings to mind: Psalm 18 beside chapter 22, Psalm 51 beside chapters 11 and 12, and Psalm 3, whose heading sets it on the day David fled from Absalom.

Do not skip the hard chapters, and do not read them alone. The chapter notes take them one at a time, say plainly what happens, and set out how careful readers have weighed them. None of those readings makes them painless.

Do not carry the book into the present as a program. It tells of Israel's king under Israel's covenant with God. It gives no nation, party or leader a warrant for violence against anyone, and no leader a shield against correction. Its own prophet walked into the palace and named the king's sin.

And read 1 Kings 1 and 2 after it, where David grows old and the question of who will follow him is settled.

hard.line: The Amalekite's story of Saul's death, which does not match 1 Samuel 31, and why David had him put to death.
David's words for Jonathan, ‘surpassing the love of women’: what they say, and how readers have understood them.
A contest at the pool of Gibeon, and a war of brother against brother.
Joab murders Abner, and David curses him but does not punish him.
The murder of Ish-bosheth, and the harsh punishment of the men who killed him.
‘The blind and the lame’: a hard saying at the taking of Jerusalem, and what it does not mean.
Why Uzzah died when he took hold of the ark.
‘I will be his Father, and he will be My son’: Solomon first, and how the New Testament reads the promise.
A throne forever, and the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC: did the promise fail?
David's harsh treatment of the Moabite prisoners, told without praise or blame.
David takes Bathsheba: the king's power, and why the text lays the guilt on him.
The letter that sent Uriah to his death.
Why the child born to Bathsheba died, and David's words, ‘I will go to him’.
The rape of Tamar, the silence pressed on her, and a father who did nothing.
Was David right to bring Absalom home without justice or repentance?
‘The LORD has told him so’: David and Shimei's curses.
Absalom and his father's concubines: ten women used as a sign of power.
Joab kills Absalom against the king's command.
Ziba or Mephibosheth: who told David the truth?
Joab murders Amasa on the road, and goes unpunished in David's lifetime.
Seven of Saul's descendants put to death for Saul's crime, and Rizpah's vigil.
Elhanan and ‘the brother of Goliath’: a verse that differs from 1 Chronicles 20:5.
How David could call himself blameless after Bathsheba and Uriah.
The LORD stirred up David to take a census, and 1 Chronicles names Satan.
Seventy thousand die for the king's sin: ‘these sheep, what have they done?’

words.line: In Hebrew bayit: a building, a palace, a temple, a household or a line of kings. David offers to build God a house, and God promises to build David one (7:11).
The Hebrew chesed: loyal, covenant-keeping love. God promises it will never be removed from David's son as it was from Saul (7:15).

In Hebrew mashiach, someone set apart by having oil poured on the head. David condemns the man who claimed to have killed the LORD's anointed (1:14), and his song ends with God's love for ‘His anointed’ (22:51). Its Greek form is Christ.
In Hebrew berit, a binding agreement sealed by oath. David makes one with the elders of Israel (5:3), and his last words call God's promise ‘an everlasting covenant’ (23:5).
In Hebrew olam, a long age. It comes eight times in chapter 7, set against Saul's short-lived line, and later readers took it at full strength.
First the Jebusite fortress David captured (5:7), then the City of David, the temple hill, Jerusalem, and God's people.
In Hebrew nagid, a leader appointed by God (5:2; 7:8). David's authority is given to him; the people remain God's.
A word for a king across the ancient world. The LORD told David, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel’ (5:2).
The gold-covered chest that stood for God's presence, called by the name of the LORD of Hosts, ‘who is enthroned between the cherubim’ (6:2).
A linen garment worn by priests. David wore one as he danced before the ark (6:14).
A wife of lower rank. Taking a ruler's concubines could be a claim to his place, which is why Abner's act (3:7) and Absalom's (16:22) were acts of power.
Shame. Saul's son Ish-bosheth and Jonathan's son Mephibosheth are called Eshbaal and Merib-baal in 1 Chronicles; scribes seem to have put this word in place of baal.
In Hebrew etsah, advice. Ahithophel's counsel was ‘like the consultation of the word of God’ (16:23), and the LORD defeated it (17:14).
In Hebrew tsur, a crag that gives shelter. David's song calls God his rock (22:2-3), and his last words call God ‘the Rock of Israel’ (23:3).
In Hebrew goren, an open place for separating grain from chaff. Araunah's floor became the site of David's altar (24:18-25) and later of the temple.

timeline.what: Saul and three of his sons die on Mount Gilboa, and David, at Ziklag, sings his lament (chapter 1).
David reigns over Judah at Hebron for seven years and six months (2:11). Saul's son Ish-bosheth reigns over the north for two years (2:10).
All Israel anoints David king at Hebron, and he takes Jerusalem (chapter 5). The dates are approximate.
Egypt is weak and Assyria not yet pressing west. David subdues the small kingdoms around Israel (chapter 8).
David takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed, and Nathan confronts him (chapters 11 and 12).

timeline.when: Two years, three years, two years
timeline.what: Absalom kills Amnon two years after Tamar is raped, stays three years in Geshur, and waits two years in Jerusalem to see the king (13:23, 38; 14:28).
Absalom's revolt (15:7, where the BSB follows some Greek copies and the Syriac; the standard Hebrew has forty).
David dies, after forty years as king (5:4), and Solomon reigns (1 Kings 2).
At Solomon's death the kingdom splits. Judah, in the south, keeps David's line of kings.

timeline.when: The second half of the 800s BC
timeline.what: An Aramaic inscription at Tel Dan, most likely set up by Hazael of Damascus, names a king of the house of David.
Babylon destroys Jerusalem, and no descendant of David rules again. Psalm 89 holds the promise of chapter 7 up to God.
The final edition of the book, on the view that it belongs to one history running from Deuteronomy to Kings.
The Greek translation divides Samuel in two. The best-preserved Samuel scroll among the Dead Sea Scrolls often agrees with the Greek.
A Dead Sea Scrolls text, 4QFlorilegium, reads 7:10-14 of the Branch of David to come.
The New Testament reads the promise of chapter 7 of Jesus (Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:30; Hebrews 1:5).
Charles Warren finds a shaft in Jerusalem, long linked with the water shaft of 5:8. Later excavations suggest it was not accessible in David's time.
Leonhard Rost argues that 2 Samuel 9 to 20 and 1 Kings 1 and 2 form one story of the succession to David's throne.
Martin Noth proposes that the books from Deuteronomy to Kings form one history, Samuel among them.
Excavations at Khirbet Qeiyafa, above the Valley of Elah, uncover a fortified town dated to the early tenth century BC.

places.name: Hebron
places.line: The men of Judah anointed David king here (2:4), and later all the elders of Israel (5:3). Absalom began his revolt here (15:10).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: The Jebusite fortress of Zion, taken by David and named the City of David (5:6-9). The ark came here (6:17), and David fled the city before Absalom (15:14).

places.name: Bethlehem
places.line: David's hometown. Asahel was buried here (2:32), and three of David's mighty men brought him water from its well (23:15-16).

places.name: Jericho
places.line: David's envoys, shamed by the Ammonite king, waited here until their beards grew back (10:5).

places.name: The Jordan
places.line: David crossed it fleeing from Absalom (17:22), and came back across it as king (19:15-18).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The land east of the Jordan. Abner made Ish-bosheth king over it (2:9), and Absalom's army camped there (17:26). Drawn roughly.

places.name: Beersheba
places.line: ‘From Dan to Beersheba’ named the whole land, north to south (3:10; 24:2).

places.name: Tyre
places.line: Hiram king of Tyre sent cedar, carpenters and stonemasons to build David's palace (5:11). The census reached the fortress of Tyre (24:7).

places.name: Sidon
places.line: Joab's census went north as far as Sidon (24:6).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: David defeated the Arameans of Damascus and put garrisons among them (8:5-6).

teaching.mapNote: Only ten places are drawn, each placed elsewhere on this site. Mahanaim, Gibeon, Rabbah, Gath, Geshur, Tekoa, Bahurim, the forest of Ephraim, Abel Beth-maacah and Dan are left off, because where they lay is debated or is not placed in this site's records. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
